summary: This Best Current Practice offers terminology for describing different kinds of Internet connectivity. Many arrangements have been sold as Internet access though they differ in what they provide, so shared terms help providers and customers compare them.

eli5.summary: People call many different things internet access. This document offers clear words so you can tell what you are actually being sold.

subtitle: A shared vocabulary so that 'Internet access' tells customers what they are really buying.

tldr.problem: Many different products are sold as 'Internet connectivity' even though they allow very different things, and there is no standard terminology to tell them apart.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines five service terms in ascending order of capability, from Web connectivity up to Full Internet Connectivity, plus a list of filtering topics and extra questions a provider can answer.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice about terminology and disclosure, not about which services should be offered. Providers SHOULD describe their service with these terms.

today: RFC 4084 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 104). The unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC.

sections.title: The Problem and the Goal
sections.content:
Providers sell many products labelled Internet or Internet access. They differ in what they allow, so one may suit a person who only browses the Web and email, and be unsuitable for someone who needs to run servers, use a virtual private network (VPN) or synchronize mail for offline use.

The RFC describes only what the service provider provides or permits. It cannot describe what user-provided equipment does. It also says the terms are meant to be non-pejorative: naming a service does not endorse it, and the Best Current Practice is about the information given to the user, not about which services should be offered.
sections.eli5: Different internet plans can do very different things. This document wants sellers to say clearly which kind they are selling, without saying one kind is bad.

sections.title: The Five Connectivity Terms
sections.content:
The terms describe the provider's intent, as shown by technical measures or terms of service. They are listed in order of ascending capability.

  • Web connectivity: access to services through a Web browser, mainly HTTP and HTTPS. Other services are generally not supported, and POP3, IMAP4 and VPNs may be unavailable. Addresses may be private, are generally dynamic and short-lived, and the provider may impose a filtering Web proxy.
  • Client connectivity only, without a public address: no support for servers or most peer-to-peer functions. The address is dynamic and usually from non-public space, so network address translation (NAT) is required. Filtering Web proxies are common and the provider SHOULD say whether one is present.
  • Client only, public address: also no servers or most peer-to-peer, but the address is public. It may not change for months, and most VPN connections work. The provider may forbid servers by contract or by filtering inbound connections.
  • Firewalled Internet Connectivity: supports most servers and peer-to-peer, with one or usually more static public addresses, but a provider-managed firewall sits in front. It is typically added at customer request and at extra cost. The provider SHOULD specify which services are blocked or intercepted.
  • Full Internet Connectivity: one or more static public addresses and no provider-imposed restrictions on ports or traffic.
sections.eli5: Think of five doors, each opening a bit wider. The first only lets you look at web pages. The last lets you do everything the internet can do.

sections.title: Full Connectivity and What It Excludes
sections.content:
For Full Internet Connectivity, filtering Web proxies, interception proxies, NAT and other provider-imposed restrictions on inbound or outbound ports and traffic are incompatible. Dynamic addresses are possible only if they last long enough to run servers without highly dynamic DNS entries, and provided they are not characterized as “dynamic” to third parties. Servers on a customer LAN are typically considered normal.

The only compatible restrictions are bandwidth limitations and prohibitions against network abuse or illegal activities.
sections.eli5: Full connectivity means the provider does not block or change your traffic. They may only limit how fast you go and stop you from doing harmful things.

sections.title: Filtering and Email Restrictions
sections.content:
Efforts to control unwanted traffic such as spam, worms and viruses have added restrictions that can apply on top of any service type. The RFC says providers should disclose the services they offer and the filters they impose. It highlights three issues.

  • Dynamic addresses: some blacklist systems assume that most undesired email comes from dynamic addresses. They identify them by provider advertising, by address-range heuristics, or by reverse-mapping names containing strings such as dsl or dial. Sometimes a missing reverse-mapping DNS record is taken as a sign. An address advertised as dynamic may be unable to send mail to arbitrary systems even with Full Internet Connectivity.
  • Non-public addresses and NATs: terms of service often prohibit systems not supplied by the provider and the operation of “servers”.
  • Outbound port filtering: some providers block external SMTP servers for message submission but permit the mail submission protocol with sender authentication (RFC 2476). Others block all outgoing messaging protocols, or divert outbound email to their own servers. If such filtering is present, especially with the public-address services, the provider MUST indicate it, and diversion MUST be disclosed because of its security and privacy implications.
sections.eli5: To stop junk mail, some providers put up fences, like blocking certain doors or sending your letters through their own mailroom. The document says they must tell you about the fences.

sections.title: Additional Terms a Provider Can Disclose
sections.content:
Section 4 lists further topics that a provider might describe and a customer might turn into questions. They are less basic than the five main terms.

  • Version support: IPv4 only, both IPv4 and IPv6, or IPv6 only.
  • Authentication support, such as unauthenticated DHCP, PPP, RADIUS or HTTP interception.
  • VPNs and tunnels: whether IPSec, L2TP or application-layer tunnels such as SSH are blocked.
  • Multicast, DNS server restrictions, and whether ICMP, ping and traceroute are blocked.
  • Roaming support, application services provided (email, Web hosting), and blocking of outbound or inbound application services.
  • Application content filtering, such as protection against worms or denial of service, spam and virus filtering, and parental-control filtering.
  • Wiretapping and interception: the service SHOULD say whether traffic is subject to lawful intercept and whether the provider will try to inform the user when that is legal.
sections.eli5: There is also a longer checklist of questions to ask a provider, such as whether you can use a VPN, which mail servers you may use, and whether anyone can listen in.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says it is about terminology, not protocols, so it raises no particular security issues. It adds that if the terminology is widely adopted, it may become easier to identify security-related expectations of particular hosts, LANs and types of connections.
sections.eli5: This is only a list of words, so it is not risky by itself. If everyone uses the words, it is easier to know what to expect from a connection.

viz.caption: THE FIVE TERMS, LOWEST TO HIGHEST CAPABILITY

items.label: Web connectivity
items.desc: Web browsing mainly; addresses may be private and short-lived.

items.label: Client only, no public address
items.desc: Dynamic non-public address behind NAT; no servers.

items.label: Client only, public address
items.desc: Public address, but servers may be prohibited.

items.label: Firewalled Internet Connectivity
items.desc: Static public addresses behind a provider-managed firewall.

items.label: Full Internet Connectivity
items.desc: Static public addresses, no provider-imposed restrictions.
